claim: Planarians undergo whole-body regeneration and tissue turnover.
source: Planarians undergo whole-body regeneration and tissue turnover, providing a model for adult positional information studies.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of planarians stated in the abstract.

claim: Genes encoding secreted and transmembrane components of multiple developmental pathways are predominantly expressed in planarian muscle cells.
source: Genes encoding secreted and transmembrane components of multiple developmental pathways are predominantly expressed in planarian muscle cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior work cited in the introduction and confirmed by the current study's findings.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing of 115 muscle cells from distinct anterior-posterior regions identified 44 regionally expressed genes.
source: Here, single-cell RNA-sequencing of 115 muscle cells from distinct anterior-posterior regions identified 44 regionally expressed genes, including multiple Wnt and ndk/FGF receptor-like (ndl/FGFRL) genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and related supplementary materials.

claim: The 44 identified regionally expressed genes include multiple Wnt and ndk/FGF receptor-like (ndl/FGFRL) genes.
source: Here, single-cell RNA-sequencing of 115 muscle cells from distinct anterior-posterior regions identified 44 regionally expressed genes, including multiple Wnt and ndk/FGF receptor-like (ndl/FGFRL) genes.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the data in Figure 1E showing the composition of the 44 genes.

claim: Two distinct FGFRL-Wnt circuits control planarian head and trunk patterning.
source: Two distinct FGFRL-Wnt circuits, involving juxtaposed anterior FGFRL and posterior Wnt expression domains, controlled planarian head and trunk patterning.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study, supported by RNAi experiments and expression analysis shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: ndl-3 and wntP-2 inhibition expanded the trunk, forming ectopic mouths and secondary pharynges.
source: ndl-3 and wntP-2 inhibition expanded the trunk, forming ectopic mouths and secondary pharynges, which independently extended and ingested food.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: Ectopic pharynges in ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi animals independently extended and ingested food.
source: ndl-3 and wntP-2 inhibition expanded the trunk, forming ectopic mouths and secondary pharynges, which independently extended and ingested food.
evidence: This functional characteristic is demonstrated in Figure 3D and Video 1.

claim: fz5/8-4 inhibition caused posterior brain expansion and ectopic eye formation.
source: fz5/8-4 inhibition, like that of ndk and wntA, caused posterior brain expansion and ectopic eye formation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5.

claim: ndk inhibition caused posterior brain expansion and ectopic eye formation.
source: fz5/8-4 inhibition, like that of ndk and wntA, caused posterior brain expansion and ectopic eye formation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 and prior literature (Cebrià et al., 2002).

claim: wntA inhibition caused posterior brain expansion and ectopic eye formation.
source: fz5/8-4 inhibition, like that of ndk and wntA, caused posterior brain expansion and ectopic eye formation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 and prior literature.

claim: FGFRL-Wnt circuits operate within a body-wide coordinate system to control adult axial positioning.
source: Our results suggest that FGFRL-Wnt circuits operate within a body-wide coordinate system to control adult axial positioning.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the combined expression and functional data.

claim: Planarians can regenerate any missing body part.
source: Planarians can regenerate any missing body part and replace aged tissues during homeostasis, presenting a powerful system for identifying adult positional information mechanisms (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about planarians, supported by citations.

claim: Planarians replace aged tissues during homeostasis.
source: Planarians can regenerate any missing body part and replace aged tissues during homeostasis, presenting a powerful system for identifying adult positional information mechanisms (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004; Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of planarians, supported by citations.

claim: Planarian regeneration requires an abundant population of dividing cells called neoblasts that includes pluripotent stem cells.
source: Planarian regeneration requires an abundant population of dividing cells called neoblasts that includes pluripotent stem cells (Wagner et al., 2011; Rink, 2013; Reddien, 2013).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about planarian biology, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Inhibition of components of the Wnt signaling pathway causes regeneration of heads in place of tails, generating two-headed animals.
source: For example, inhibition of components of the Wnt signaling pathway causes regeneration of heads in place of tails, generating two-headed animals with heads facing opposing directions (Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Gurley et al., 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a well-documented phenotype in planarian research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Wnt-signaling inhibition causes hypercephalized planarians during tissue turnover.
source: Several striking planarian phenotypes associated with altered regional tissue identity during tissue turnover have also been identified, including hypercephalized (Wnt-signaling inhibition) (Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Gurley et al., 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008) and ventralized (BMP-signaling inhibition) (Reddien et al., 2007; Molina et al., 2007; Orii and Watanabe, 2007) planarians.
evidence: This is a known phenotype from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: BMP-signaling inhibition causes ventralized planarians during tissue turnover.
source: Several striking planarian phenotypes associated with altered regional tissue identity during tissue turnover have also been identified, including hypercephalized (Wnt-signaling inhibition) (Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Gurley et al., 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008) and ventralized (BMP-signaling inhibition) (Reddien et al., 2007; Molina et al., 2007; Orii and Watanabe, 2007) planarians.
evidence: This is a known phenotype from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Wnt regulates anterior-posterior axis development in many animal phyla.
source: Reminiscent of the roles of Wnt and Bmp in planarian regeneration and tissue turnover, Wnt regulates anterior-posterior (AP) axis development (Petersen and Reddien, 2009b; Niehrs, 2010) and Bmp regulates dorsal-ventral (DV) axis development (De Robertis and Sasai, 1996) in many animal phyla.
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology, supported by citations.

claim: Bmp regulates dorsal-ventral axis development in many animal phyla.
source: Reminiscent of the roles of Wnt and Bmp in planarian regeneration and tissue turnover, Wnt regulates anterior-posterior (AP) axis development (Petersen and Reddien, 2009b; Niehrs, 2010) and Bmp regulates dorsal-ventral (DV) axis development (De Robertis and Sasai, 1996) in many animal phyla.
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology, supported by a citation.

claim: Receptors, ligands, and secreted inhibitors of BMP and Wnt pathways are constitutively expressed in a regionalized manner across adult planarian body axes.
source: Many receptors, ligands, and secreted inhibitors belonging to key pathways that regulate development in many organisms, such as BMP and Wnt pathways are constitutively expressed in a regionalized manner across adult planarian body axes (Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact, supported by a citation.

claim: Patterning genes in planarians are predominantly expressed together in body-wall muscle.
source: Interestingly, these genes are predominantly expressed together in the same planarian tissue, the body-wall muscle (Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a key finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Expression patterns of patterning genes can change dynamically following injury in planarians.
source: Expression patterns of these genes can change dynamically following injury (Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2009a; Gurley et al., 2010; Witchley et al., 2013), and some of these changes can occur in existing muscle cells in the absence of neoblasts (Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a known phenomenon from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Some expression pattern changes in muscle can occur in existing muscle cells in the absence of neoblasts.
source: Expression patterns of these genes can change dynamically following injury (Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2009a; Gurley et al., 2010; Witchley et al., 2013), and some of these changes can occur in existing muscle cells in the absence of neoblasts (Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a specific finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Body-wall muscle is distributed peripherally around the entire planarian body.
source: Body-wall muscle is distributed peripherally around the entire planarian body, and the known expression domains of candidate patterning molecules in muscle broadly span the AP, DV, and medial-lateral (ML) body axes, raising the possibility that muscle provides a body-wide coordinate system of positional information that controls regional tissue identity in tissue turnover and regeneration (Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact about planarians, supported by a citation.

claim: Expression domains of candidate patterning molecules in muscle broadly span the AP, DV, and medial-lateral body axes.
source: Body-wall muscle is distributed peripherally around the entire planarian body, and the known expression domains of candidate patterning molecules in muscle broadly span the AP, DV, and medial-lateral (ML) body axes, raising the possibility that muscle provides a body-wide coordinate system of positional information that controls regional tissue identity in tissue turnover and regeneration (Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Muscle may provide a body-wide coordinate system of positional information that controls regional tissue identity in tissue turnover and regeneration.
source: Body-wall muscle is distributed peripherally around the entire planarian body, and the known expression domains of candidate patterning molecules in muscle broadly span the AP, DV, and medial-lateral (ML) body axes, raising the possibility that muscle provides a body-wide coordinate system of positional information that controls regional tissue identity in tissue turnover and regeneration (Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis raised based on prior observations, supported by a citation.

claim: Non-dividing single cells from 10 consecutive regions along the AP axis were isolated by fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS).
source: Non-dividing single cells from 10 consecutive regions along the AP axis (Figure 1A) were isolated by fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS), and the resulting single-cell cDNA libraries were screened by qRT-PCR for expression of planarian muscle markers before sequencing (Methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Single-cell cDNA libraries were screened by qRT-PCR for expression of planarian muscle markers before sequencing.
source: Non-dividing single cells from 10 consecutive regions along the AP axis (Figure 1A) were isolated by fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS), and the resulting single-cell cDNA libraries were screened by qRT-PCR for expression of planarian muscle markers before sequencing (Methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Cells expressed an average of 3,253 transcripts.
source: Cells expressed an average of 3,253 transcripts, within the range reported for planarian single-cell libraries (Wurtzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the sequencing data.

claim: The average number of transcripts expressed per cell is within the range reported for planarian single-cell libraries.
source: Cells expressed an average of 3,253 transcripts, within the range reported for planarian single-cell libraries (Wurtzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This comparison is made to prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Principal component analysis identified two significant principal components that separated cells by expression of muscle markers and neoblast markers.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) on the 177 single cells sequenced was performed using highly variable transcripts. Two significant principal components that separated cells by expression of muscle markers (PC1<0) and expression of neoblast markers (PC2<0) were identified (details in Methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This describes the results of the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 115 muscle cells were identified by PCA and troponin expression.
source: PCA and troponin expression confirmed the identity of 115 muscle cells, and these 115 cells were used in all subsequent analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This describes the cell selection process for the study.

claim: 26 of the 44 regionally expressed genes identified were previously not reported to be regionally expressed in muscle.
source: ISH analysis verified 44 of these genes as regionally expressed (35/44 with p<0.005 in any of anterior-versus-posterior SCDE analyses) from the total 256 genes tested, including 26 previously not reported to be regionally expressed in muscle (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: This quantifies the novel findings of the study.

claim: All newly identified regionally expressed genes tested were expressed at least in part in cells expressing the planarian muscle marker collagen.
source: All newly identified regionally expressed genes tested were expressed at least in part in cells expressing the planarian muscle marker collagen (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by double FISH experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the average expression per region of the 44 mRGs recapitulates the AP order of the regions.
source: Hierarchical clustering of the average expression per region of the 44 mRGs identified recapitulates the AP order of the regions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and demonstrates the spatial coherence of the expression patterns.

claim: The 44 identified mRGs were comprised mainly of genes encoding Wnt-signaling components, Hox-family transcription factors, and fibroblast growth factor receptor-like (FGFRL) proteins.
source: Interestingly, the 44 identified mRGs identified here were comprised mainly of genes encoding Wnt-signaling components, Hox-family transcription factors, and fibroblast growth factor receptor-like (FGFRL) proteins (Figure 1E), suggesting that these gene families have prominent roles in providing positional information for maintaining and regenerating the planarian primary body axis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and leads to an inference about their roles.

claim: Wnt, Hox, and FGFRL gene families have prominent roles in providing positional information for maintaining and regenerating the planarian primary body axis.
source: Interestingly, the 44 identified mRGs identified here were comprised mainly of genes encoding Wnt-signaling components, Hox-family transcription factors, and fibroblast growth factor receptor-like (FGFRL) proteins (Figure 1E), suggesting that these gene families have prominent roles in providing positional information for maintaining and regenerating the planarian primary body axis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the composition of the identified genes and their functional analysis.

claim: Planarians have six FGFRL-encoding genes.
source: Planarians have six FGFRL-encoding genes, named nou darake (ndk), the defining member of the FGFRL family (Cebrià et al., 2002), and nou darake-like (ndl)-1 through ndl-5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All six planarian FGFRL genes were identified in the SCDE analyses as AP mRGs.
source: All of these FGFRL genes were identified in the SCDE analyses as AP mRGs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At least three of the five FGFRL genes with expression at the anterior-most region were co-expressed in all 11 muscle cells isolated from the anterior head tip.
source: At least three of the five FGFRL genes with expression at the anterior-most region of the animal (ndk, ndl-1, ndl-2, ndl-4, ndl-5) were co-expressed in all 11 muscle cells isolated and sequenced from the anterior head tip (region 1); 10/11 of these cells also co-expressed ndk and frizzled5/8–4 (fz5/8–4) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 2B.

claim: 10 out of 11 muscle cells from the anterior head tip co-expressed ndk and frizzled5/8-4.
source: At least three of the five FGFRL genes with expression at the anterior-most region of the animal (ndk, ndl-1, ndl-2, ndl-4, ndl-5) were co-expressed in all 11 muscle cells isolated and sequenced from the anterior head tip (region 1); 10/11 of these cells also co-expressed ndk and frizzled5/8–4 (fz5/8–4) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 2B.

claim: In single muscle cells from the pre-pharyngeal region, 3 out of 6 cells expressing ndl-3 also expressed wntP-2.
source: In the single muscle cells sequenced from the pre-pharyngeal region (region 4), 3/6 cells expressing ndl-3 also expressed wntP-2.
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 2B.

claim: FISH demonstrated co-expression of FGFRL and Wnt-pathway genes together in the same cells in regions where their expression domains overlapped.
source: FISH also demonstrated co-expression of FGFRL and Wnt-pathway genes together in the same cells in regions where their expression domains overlapped (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Extensive co-expression of multiple mRGs in single muscle cells was observed in different regions along the entire AP axis.
source: Similarly, extensive co-expression of multiple mRGs in single muscle cells was observed in different regions along the entire AP axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: β-catenin-1 RNAi animals develop ectopic heads around the entire body during tissue turnover.
source: Wnt signaling is also required for maintenance of the AP axis, with β-catenin-1 RNAi animals developing ectopic heads around the entire body during tissue turnover (Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Gurley et al., 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a known phenotype from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: At early timepoints following β-catenin-1 RNAi, animals showed subtle posterior expansions of ndl-5 and ndl-2 expression domains.
source: At early timepoints following RNAi (7–9 days after first RNAi feeding), β-catenin-1 RNAi animals showed subtle posterior expansions of ndl-5 and ndl-2 expression domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ectopic expression of ndl-5 in β-catenin-1 RNAi animals occurred in posterior and lateral locations and preceded ectopic expression of ndl-2.
source: Later, ectopic expression of ndl-5 in posterior and lateral locations occurred and preceded ectopic expression of ndl-2 (9 days after first RNAi feeding) even before the appearance of ectopic eyes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fully formed ectopic heads in β-catenin-1 RNAi animals showed clear ectopic expression of the pre-pharyngeal mRG ndl-3.
source: Fully formed ectopic heads (21 days after first RNAi feeding) showed clear ectopic expression of the pre-pharyngeal mRG ndl-3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Gross anatomical changes in the AP axis are accompanied by corresponding changes in FGFRL expression domains.
source: Gross anatomical changes in the AP axis are therefore accompanied by corresponding changes in FGFRL expression domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the β-catenin-1 RNAi experiments showing coordinated changes in anatomy and gene expression.

claim: The axial expression map of genes in planarian adult muscle is reminiscent of regionalized gene expression patterns found during embryonic development in other species.
source: The axial expression map of genes in planarian adult muscle is reminiscent of regionalized gene expression patterns found during embryonic development in other species (Pankratz and Jäckle, 1993; De Robertis et al., 2000; Jaeger et al., 2012) and provides a tool to dissect adult positional identity maintenance and regeneration.
evidence: This is a comparison to known developmental biology patterns, supported by citations.

claim: Inhibition of single or combinations of Hox genes did not result in animals with a robust abnormal phenotype.
source: Inhibition of single or combinations of Hox genes and a subset of FGFRL genes (ndl-1, ndl-2, ndl-4, and ndl-5) did not result in animals with a robust abnormal phenotype (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is a negative result from the RNAi screen reported in Supplementary file 1G.

claim: Inhibition of a subset of FGFRL genes (ndl-1, ndl-2, ndl-4, and ndl-5) did not result in animals with a robust abnormal phenotype.
source: Inhibition of single or combinations of Hox genes and a subset of FGFRL genes (ndl-1, ndl-2, ndl-4, and ndl-5) did not result in animals with a robust abnormal phenotype (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This is a negative result from the RNAi screen reported in Supplementary file 1G.

claim: Expression of other members of the FGFRL family was not affected by ndl-1, ndl-2, ndl-4, and ndl-5 RNAi at the time-point analyzed.
source: Additionally, expression of other members of the FGFRL family was not affected under these RNAi conditions at the time-point analyzed (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The ndl-3 gene is expressed from below the eyes to the esophagus at the anterior end of the pharynx.
source: The ndl-3 gene is expressed from below the eyes to the esophagus at the anterior end of the pharynx (Figure 1B, [Rink et al., 2009]), which is located centrally in the animal trunk (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by a citation.

claim: ndl-3 RNAi resulted in the formation of two or more mouths and two pharynges.
source: ndl-3 RNAi resulted in a striking phenotype: the formation of two or more mouths and two pharynges (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ectopic mouths and pharynges of ndl-3 RNAi animals appeared within the trunk, posterior to the original mouth/pharynx location.
source: The ectopic mouths and pharynges of ndl-3 RNAi animals appeared within the trunk, posterior to the original mouth/pharynx location.
evidence: This describes the location of the ectopic structures observed in Figure 3.

claim: The ectopic mouth/pharynx phenotype in ndl-3 RNAi animals emerged both during tissue turnover in uninjured animals and following regeneration.
source: This phenotype emerged both during tissue turnover in uninjured animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and following regeneration (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In regenerating ndl-3 RNAi animals, animals initially regenerated a single mouth/pharynx, but as regenerating animals grew following feeding, ectopic mouths and pharynges emerged.
source: In the case of regeneration, animals initially regenerated a single mouth/pharynx, but as regenerating animals grew following feeding, ectopic mouths and pharynges emerged.
evidence: This describes the temporal progression of the phenotype during regeneration.

claim: Inhibition of wntP-2 caused ectopic mouth and pharynx formation.
source: Inhibition of the posterior mRG wntP-2/wnt11-5 also caused ectopic mouth and pharynx formation (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), in agreement with a recent report (Sureda-Gómez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and supported by a citation to a recent report.

claim: Double RNAi of ndl-3 and wntP-2 was synergistic.
source: Double RNAi of ndl-3 and wntP-2 was synergistic (Figure 3A, Fisher's exact test p<0.0001 for ndl-3, p=0.0153 for wntP-2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inhibition of ndl-3 and wntP-2 resulted in pharyngeal cavity expansion.
source: Inhibition of ndl-3 and wntP-2 also resulted in pharyngeal cavity expansion (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and in increased numbers of para-pharyngeal cells (Figure 3B), which express the matrix metalloproteinase mmp1 (Newmark et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of ndl-3 and wntP-2 resulted in increased numbers of para-pharyngeal cells.
source: Inhibition of ndl-3 and wntP-2 also resulted in pharyngeal cavity expansion (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and in increased numbers of para-pharyngeal cells (Figure 3B), which express the matrix metalloproteinase mmp1 (Newmark et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Para-pharyngeal cells express the matrix metalloproteinase mmp1.
source: Inhibition of ndl-3 and wntP-2 also resulted in pharyngeal cavity expansion (Figure 3B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and in increased numbers of para-pharyngeal cells (Figure 3B), which express the matrix metalloproteinase mmp1 (Newmark et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact, supported by a citation.

claim: The planarian pharynx is a long muscular organ that can extend through the mouth to ingest food.
source: The planarian pharynx is a long muscular organ that can extend through the mouth to ingest food (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004) and connects to the intestine through the esophagus at the medial anterior end of the pharyngeal cavity.
evidence: This is a known anatomical fact about planarians, supported by a citation.

claim: The planarian pharynx connects to the intestine through the esophagus at the medial anterior end of the pharyngeal cavity.
source: The planarian pharynx is a long muscular organ that can extend through the mouth to ingest food (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004) and connects to the intestine through the esophagus at the medial anterior end of the pharyngeal cavity.
evidence: This is a known anatomical fact about planarians.

claim: In ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi animals, ectopic esophagi formed in variable locations.
source: In ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi animals, ectopic esophagi (NB.22.1e+) formed in variable locations, including from the side of the pharyngeal cavity wall and from a gut branch crossing the pharyngeal cavity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Despite variable positioning, ectopic pharynges in ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi animals always integrated through an esophagus into the intestine.
source: Despite variable positioning, ectopic pharynges always integrated through an esophagus into the intestine, demonstrating remarkable plasticity in the mechanisms underlying tissue organization.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3C and demonstrates tissue organization plasticity.

claim: Ectopic pharynges in ndl-3; wntP-2 RNAi or wntP-2 RNAi animals were functional.
source: Ectopic pharynges in ndl-3; wntP-2 RNAi or wntP-2 RNAi animals were also functional – animals simultaneously projected both pharynges and each pharynx displayed independent food searching behavior, such as on opposite sides of the animal or in different directions (Figure 3D, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3D and Video 1.

claim: Animals with ectopic pharynges simultaneously projected both pharynges and each pharynx displayed independent food searching behavior.
source: Ectopic pharynges in ndl-3; wntP-2 RNAi or wntP-2 RNAi animals were also functional – animals simultaneously projected both pharynges and each pharynx displayed independent food searching behavior, such as on opposite sides of the animal or in different directions (Figure 3D, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3D and Video 1.

claim: Anterior-most mRG expression domains (sFRP-1 and ndl-5) showed no overt changes following ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi.
source: Anterior-most mRG expression domains (sFRP-1 and ndl-5) were present and showed no overt changes following ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ndl-3 expression domain was expanded to the ectopic posterior esophagus in wntP-2 RNAi animals.
source: By contrast, the ndl-3 expression domain was expanded to the ectopic posterior esophagus in wntP-2 RNAi animals (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A,D.

claim: In wntP-2 and ndl-3; wntP-2 RNAi animals, the expression domain of sFRP-2 was extended towards the animal posterior.
source: In both wntP-2 and ndl-3; wntP-2 RNAi animals, the expression domain of sFRP-2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) was also extended towards the animal posterior.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Expression of the pre-pharyngeal mRGs wnt2 and ndl-2 was changed only slightly or not at all in ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi animals.
source: By contrast, expression of the pre-pharyngeal mRGs wnt2 and ndl-2 was changed only slightly or not at all (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The broad posterior expression domain of wntP-2 was significantly reduced in ndl-3 RNAi animals.
source: Conversely, the broad posterior expression domain of wntP-2 was significantly reduced in ndl-3 RNAi animals (Figure 4B,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B,E.

claim: Expression of posterior mRGs fz4-1 and dd_13065 was still present in ndl-3, wntP-2, and ndl3; wntP-2 RNAi animals.
source: Expression of other posterior mRGs such as fz4-1 and dd_13065 was still present in ndl-3, wntP-2, and ndl3; wntP-2 RNAi animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: ndl-3 and wntP-2 are required for maintaining normal trunk tissue pattern including associated mRG expression domains, but not head or tail patterns of mRG expression.
source: Thus, both ndl-3 and wntP-2 are required for maintaining normal trunk tissue pattern including associated mRG expression domains, but not head or tail patterns of mRG expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective changes in mRG expression shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The trunk patterning defects of ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi animals only affect local mRG expression within the axial map.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that the trunk patterning defects of ndl-3 and wntP-2 RNAi animals only affect local mRG expression within the axial map.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only trunk-region mRGs are affected, not head or tail mRGs.

claim: fz5/8-4 RNAi caused ectopic eye formation and expansion of the brain posteriorly in both uninjured and regenerating animals.
source: In addition to trunk patterning phenotypes, we found that fz5/8–4 RNAi caused ectopic eye formation and expansion of the brain posteriorly in both uninjured and regenerating animals (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: fz5/8-4 showed graded anterior expression, strongest at the head tip, and brain expression.
source: fz5/8–4 showed graded anterior expression, strongest at the head tip, and brain expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The fz5/8-4 RNAi phenotype was similar to that previously described for ndk and wntA RNAi.
source: The fz5/8–4 RNAi phenotype was similar to that previously described for ndk and wntA RNAi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, [Cebrià et al., 2002; Kobayashi et al., 2007; Adell et al., 2009; Hill and Petersen, 2015]).
evidence: This comparison is made to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: ndk is expressed in head muscle and the brain.
source: ndk is expressed in head muscle and the brain (Figure 1B, [Cebrià et al., 2002; Witchley et al., 2013]) and restricts brain tissues to the animal head (Cebrià et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by citations.

claim: ndk restricts brain tissues to the animal head.
source: ndk is expressed in head muscle and the brain (Figure 1B, [Cebrià et al., 2002; Witchley et al., 2013]) and restricts brain tissues to the animal head (Cebrià et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a known function from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: wntA is expressed broadly, with strong expression at the posterior base of the brain.
source: wntA is expressed broadly, with strong expression at the posterior base of the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, [Kobayashi et al., 2007; Adell et al., 2009; Hill and Petersen, 2015]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and supported by citations.

claim: wntA; ndk double RNAi animals showed a stronger phenotype in homeostasis than did single gene RNAi animals.
source: wntA; ndk double RNAi animals showed a stronger phenotype in homeostasis (Figure 5A,B) and regeneration (Kobayashi et al., 2007), than did single gene RNAi animals.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A,B and supported by a citation for regeneration.

claim: Double RNAi of fz5/8-4 and either ndk or wntA showed a synergistic effect during tissue turnover.
source: Double RNAi of fz5/8–4 and either ndk or wntA also showed a synergistic effect during tissue turnover (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Fisher's exact test p<0.0001 for both ndk and wntA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RNAi of four out of five other ndl (FGFRL)-family members further enhanced the fz5/8-4; ndk double RNAi phenotype.
source: Additionally, RNAi of four out of five other ndl (FGFRL)-family members further enhanced the fz5/8–4; ndk double RNAi phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1G), suggesting that multiple FGFRL genes synergize to control head pattern with ndk.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1G.

claim: Multiple FGFRL genes synergize to control head pattern with ndk.
source: Additionally, RNAi of four out of five other ndl (FGFRL)-family members further enhanced the fz5/8–4; ndk double RNAi phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1G), suggesting that multiple FGFRL genes synergize to control head pattern with ndk.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhancement of the phenotype by multiple FGFRL RNAi.

claim: Following eight RNAi feedings, fz5/8-4; ndk, wntA; ndk, and fz5/8-4; wntA double RNAi intact animals showed posterior expansion of multiple neuron classes from different head regions.
source: Following eight RNAi feedings, fz5/8–4; ndk, wntA; ndk, and fz5/8–4; wntA double RNAi intact animals showed posterior expansion of multiple neuron classes from different head regions suggesting that the entire head-restricted nervous system expanded posteriorly (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The entire head-restricted nervous system expanded posteriorly in fz5/8-4; ndk, wntA; ndk, and fz5/8-4; wntA double RNAi animals.
source: Following eight RNAi feedings, fz5/8–4; ndk, wntA; ndk, and fz5/8–4; wntA double RNAi intact animals showed posterior expansion of multiple neuron classes from different head regions suggesting that the entire head-restricted nervous system expanded posteriorly (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple neuron classes from different head regions expanded posteriorly.

claim: After eight RNAi feedings, non-neural mag-1+ adhesive gland cells showed normal distribution in fz5/8-4; ndk and wntA; ndk RNAi animals.
source: After eight RNAi feedings, a time point at which brain expansion was visible, non-neural mag-1+ adhesive gland cells (Zayas et al., 2010) showed normal distribution (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By 12 RNAi feedings, mag-1+ cells were disorganized in fz5/8-4; ndk and wntA; ndk RNAi animals.
source: By 12 RNAi feedings, however, mag-1+ cells were disorganized (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), indicating that non-neural head cell types were eventually affected, but not visibly posteriorized, by these RNAi conditions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Non-neural head cell types were eventually affected, but not visibly posteriorized, by fz5/8-4; ndk and wntA; ndk RNAi.
source: By 12 RNAi feedings, however, mag-1+ cells were disorganized (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), indicating that non-neural head cell types were eventually affected, but not visibly posteriorized, by these RNAi conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the disorganization of mag-1+ cells without obvious posteriorization.

claim: Anterior-most (sFRP-1 and ndl-4) and posterior (wntP-2, wnt11-1, and wnt11-2) mRG expression domains did not visibly change in fz5/8-4; ndk RNAi or wntA; ndk double RNAi animals.
source: Anterior-most (sFRP-1 and ndl-4) and posterior (wntP-2, wnt11-1, and wnt11-2) mRG expression domains did not visibly change in fz5/8–4; ndk RNAi or wntA; ndk double RNAi animals, even under strong RNAi conditions (12 RNAi feedings, multiple ectopic eyes) (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: ndl-2 expression was expanded into the pre-pharyngeal region after eight RNAi feedings in fz5/8-4; ndk and wntA; ndk RNAi animals.
source: By contrast, ndl-2 expression, which is normally restricted to a domain immediately posterior to the eyes, was expanded into the pre-pharyngeal region after eight RNAi feedings (Figure 6B,E), and showed a more severe posterior expansion after 12 RNAi feedings (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ndl-5, ndk, and wnt2 expression domains extended posteriorly into the pre-pharyngeal region in RNAi animals with strong phenotypes.
source: Similarly, ndl-5, ndk, and wnt2 expression domains extended posteriorly into the pre-pharyngeal region in RNAi animals with strong phenotypes (Figure 6A,D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,E.

claim: The anterior end of the pre-pharyngeal ndl-3 expression domain was significantly posterior-shifted in fz5/8-4; ndk and wntA; ndk RNAi animals.
source: By contrast, the anterior end of the pre-pharyngeal ndl-3 expression domain was significantly posterior-shifted (Figure 6C,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C,F.

claim: ndk, wntA, and fz5/8-4 are required to restrict anterior tissues and associated expression domains of mRGs to the head region, while leaving the anterior tip, trunk, and tail mRG domains unaffected.
source: Our results indicate that ndk, wntA, and fz5/8–4 are required to restrict anterior tissues and associated expression domains of mRGs to the head region, while leaving the anterior tip, trunk, and tail mRG domains unaffected.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective changes in mRG expression shown in Figure 6.

claim: Planarian muscle was previously found to express several genes with known roles in adult tissue patterning in planarians.
source: Planarian muscle was previously found to express several genes with known roles in adult tissue patterning in planarians, raising the possibility that muscle functions to produce a body-wide coordinate system of positional information (Witchley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Traditional RNA sequencing approaches to identifying candidate adult positional information in planarians is limited by the diversity of gene expression in heterogeneous tissue.
source: Traditional RNA sequencing approaches to identifying candidate adult positional information in planarians is limited by the diversity of gene expression in heterogeneous tissue.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of traditional approaches.

claim: The identification of a particular cell type expressing genes associated with regional tissue identity allowed application of regional single-cell sequencing to surmount the challenge of tissue heterogeneity.
source: The identification of a particular cell type expressing genes associated with regional tissue identity allowed application of regional single-cell sequencing to surmount this challenge.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Coordinate systems of positional information might exist within adult tissues of many animals, including humans.
source: Coordinate systems of positional information, such as those proposed to control embryonic development (De Robertis et al., 2000; Petersen and Reddien, 2009b; Niehrs, 2010), might exist within adult tissues of many animals, including humans (Rinn et al., 2006), however there is little functional data regarding positional information and maintenance of the adult body plan.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior work, supported by citations.

claim: There is little functional data regarding positional information and maintenance of the adult body plan.
source: Coordinate systems of positional information, such as those proposed to control embryonic development (De Robertis et al., 2000; Petersen and Reddien, 2009b; Niehrs, 2010), might exist within adult tissues of many animals, including humans (Rinn et al., 2006), however there is little functional data regarding positional information and maintenance of the adult body plan.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Both the planarian head and trunk require an FGFRL-Wnt circuit to maintain adult regional tissue identity.
source: Here we show that both the planarian head and trunk require an FGFRL-Wnt circuit to maintain adult regional tissue identity.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study, supported by the functional data in Figures 3-6.

claim: Different FGFRL and Wnt genes are used in the two body locations (head and trunk).
source: Different FGFRL and Wnt genes are used in the two body locations; however, in both cases, an FGFRL expression domain is juxtaposed by a posterior Wnt expression domain.
evidence: This is shown by the expression analysis in Figure 2 and the functional analysis in Figures 3-6.

claim: In both head and trunk FGFRL-Wnt circuits, an FGFRL expression domain is juxtaposed by a posterior Wnt expression domain.
source: Different FGFRL and Wnt genes are used in the two body locations; however, in both cases, an FGFRL expression domain is juxtaposed by a posterior Wnt expression domain.
evidence: This is shown by the expression analysis in Figure 2 and Figure 7C.

claim: Inhibition of either gene (FGFRL or Wnt) in the two circuits caused posterior expansion and sequential duplications of structures normally found within the head and trunk regions.
source: Strikingly, inhibition of either gene (FGFRL or Wnt) caused posterior expansion and sequential duplications of structures normally found within the head and trunk regions, resulting in expanded brain and ectopic eyes in one case, and ectopic pharynges and mouths in the other (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Following inhibition of any of the components of these FGFRL-Wnt circuits, the axial expression map shows local shifts in expression domains coincident with the expansion of specific regionally restricted tissues.
source: Following inhibition of any of the components of these FGFRL-Wnt circuits, the axial expression map shows local shifts in expression domains coincident with the expansion of specific regionally restricted tissues such as brain and pharynx (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Muscle marks different AP regions through combinatorial expression of mRGs.
source: These results suggest that muscle, a tissue found uniformly throughout the animal, marks different AP regions through combinatorial expression of mRGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression analysis in Figure 2 showing combinatorial expression of mRGs in muscle cells.

claim: Communication exists between muscle cells and the underlying region-specific tissues.
source: This implies that communication exists between muscle cells and the underlying region-specific tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that muscle expresses patterning genes and regional tissues are affected by their inhibition.

claim: Positional information must be integrated into the decision to generate and pattern new tissue during planarian growth and regeneration.
source: Positional information must be integrated into the decision to generate and pattern new tissue during planarian growth and regeneration.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how positional information functions in planarians.

claim: mRGs might influence the regional behavior of neoblasts and/or their division progeny.
source: mRGs might therefore influence the regional behavior of neoblasts and/or their division progeny.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism by which mRGs affect tissue patterning.

claim: The two FGFRL-Wnt circuits described in this work are striking examples of body plan plasticity during homeostatic tissue turnover.
source: The two FGFRL-Wnt circuits described in this work are striking examples of body plan plasticity during homeostatic tissue turnover.
evidence: This is a characterization of the findings based on the observation that ectopic structures form during tissue turnover.

claim: In both FGFRL-Wnt circuits, inhibition by RNAi of FGFRL genes and inhibition of Wnt pathway components are coincident with the same phenotype of expanded regional identity.
source: In both cases, inhibition by RNAi of FGFRL genes (i.e., reduction or absence of the FGFRL expression domain) and inhibition of Wnt pathway components (i.e., expansion of the FGFRL expression domain) are coincident with the same phenotype of expanded regional identity.
evidence: This is observed in the RNAi experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: FGFRL proteins confine the regions where specific tissues in both the head and trunk can normally form.
source: We propose that FGFRL proteins confine the regions where specific tissues in both the head and trunk can normally form and that the Wnt gene of each circuit acts by restricting tissues at the anterior end of its expression domain (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the expression and functional data.

claim: The Wnt gene of each FGFRL-Wnt circuit acts by restricting tissues at the anterior end of its expression domain.
source: We propose that FGFRL proteins confine the regions where specific tissues in both the head and trunk can normally form and that the Wnt gene of each circuit acts by restricting tissues at the anterior end of its expression domain (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the expression and functional data.

claim: FGFRL-Wnt circuits might be broadly utilized, but presently underappreciated, patterning modules of animal body plans.
source: Given the similarities of the distinct FGFRL-Wnt circuits for patterning two different body regions, FGFRL-Wnt circuits might be broadly utilized, but presently underappreciated, patterning modules of animal body plans.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: Asexual Schmidtea mediterranea strain (CIW4) animals starved 7–14 days prior to experiments were used.
source: Asexual Schmidtea mediterranea strain (CIW4) animals starved 7–14 days prior experiments were used.
evidence: This describes the experimental animals used in the study.
